history.heading: Gaul and the Franks
paragraphs: France has been inhabited since prehistoric times; the cave paintings of Lascaux, around 17,000 years old, are among the most famous examples of Palaeolithic art. In antiquity the region was home to Celtic peoples known as the Gauls, whom Julius Caesar conquered in the 50s BCE. Roman Gaul became prosperous, with cities such as Lyon and Nîmes.

After Rome's fall, the Franks, a Germanic people, established a kingdom. Their king Clovis converted to Christianity around 500, and Charlemagne was crowned emperor in 800, ruling much of Western Europe. The western part of his empire became the Kingdom of France.

history.heading: The kingdom of France
paragraphs: The Capetian dynasty, from 987, gradually built a strong monarchy around Paris. The Hundred Years' War with England (1337–1453) saw Joan of Arc rally French forces. Gothic cathedrals such as Notre-Dame and Chartres were built in this period.

In the 16th century wars of religion between Catholics and Protestants (Huguenots) devastated the country until the Edict of Nantes in 1598. Louis XIV, the "Sun King", built the Palace of Versailles and made France Europe's dominant power. The Enlightenment philosophers Voltaire, Rousseau and Montesquieu spread new ideas.

history.heading: Revolution and Napoleon
paragraphs: The French Revolution of 1789 overthrew the absolute monarchy, proclaimed the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, and abolished feudal privileges. King Louis XVI was executed in 1793, and the Terror followed.

Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in 1799, crowned himself emperor in 1804 and conquered much of Europe, spreading the Napoleonic Code. He was defeated at Waterloo in 1815. The 19th century brought alternating monarchies, empires and republics, industrialisation and a large colonial empire in Africa and Asia.

history.heading: World wars and the Fifth Republic
paragraphs: France was a main battleground of the First World War, with immense losses at battles such as Verdun. In 1940 Nazi Germany occupied France; the collaborationist Vichy regime helped deport Jews, while the Resistance and Charles de Gaulle's Free French fought on.

After the war, France was a founding member of the European communities. Decolonisation brought wars in Indochina and Algeria, which led to the founding of the Fifth Republic under de Gaulle in 1958. May 1968 protests transformed society. France helped create the European Union and the euro.

culture.heading: Language and ideas
paragraphs: French is the official language and is spoken by hundreds of millions of people worldwide; the Académie française has overseen it since 1635. Regional languages include Breton, Occitan, Basque, Corsican and Alsatian.

France has a strong tradition of secularism (laïcité). Catholicism is the largest religion by tradition, and France has Europe's largest Muslim and Jewish communities. French thinkers, from Descartes to Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir and Foucault, have shaped world philosophy.

culture.heading: Arts and literature
paragraphs: France has produced towering figures in literature, such as Molière, Victor Hugo, Balzac, Flaubert, Proust and Camus, and more Nobel laureates in literature than any other country. In art, Impressionism (Monet, Renoir, Degas) and later movements such as Cubism developed in France, and Paris was the art capital of the world.
The Louvre is the world's most visited museum, and France invented cinema with the Lumière brothers. The Cannes Film Festival is the most prestigious film festival.

culture.heading: Food, fashion and sport
paragraphs: The French gastronomic meal is recognised by UNESCO. France is famous for its wines (Bordeaux, Burgundy, Champagne), hundreds of cheeses, bread such as the baguette (also on the UNESCO list) and pastries. Paris is a world capital of fashion and luxury, home to houses such as Chanel, Dior and Louis Vuitton.
The Tour de France is the world's most famous cycling race. Football is the most popular sport; France won the World Cup in 1998 and 2018. Paris hosted the Olympic Games in 2024.

politics.heading: Semi-presidential republic
paragraphs: The Fifth Republic is a semi-presidential system. The president, elected directly for five years, is powerful, especially in foreign policy and defence, and appoints the prime minister, who must have the support of the National Assembly. Parliament also includes the Senate.

After the 2024 snap elections produced a parliament split between left, centre and far-right blocs with no majority, governments have been unstable. The far-right National Rally has become one of the largest parties.

politics.heading: Global role
paragraphs: France is a permanent member of the UN Security Council, a nuclear power, a founding member of the EU and NATO, and a member of the G7. It has overseas departments and territories around the world, giving it the world's second-largest exclusive economic zone. Its influence in its former African colonies has declined, with French troops leaving several Sahel countries.

economy.heading: A major economy
paragraphs: France has one of the world's largest economies. Key sectors include aerospace (Airbus is based in Toulouse), luxury goods, cars, pharmaceuticals, agriculture and food, energy and finance. France is the world's most visited country, with around 100 million international tourists a year.
About 70 percent of its electricity comes from nuclear power, the highest share of any country. The currency is the euro.

economy.heading: Challenges
paragraphs: France has a generous welfare state and high public spending and taxes. Public debt and the budget deficit are high, contributing to political crises over budget cuts. Reforms such as raising the pension age to 64 in 2023 provoked mass protests. Unemployment, especially among young people, and regional inequalities are persistent concerns.
